query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of boron (0.5–1.0 wt%) during alloy processing will result in boron segregation to the lamellar colony interfaces, enhancing their cohesion and thereby improving both tensile strength and room-temperature ductility compared to the unmodified alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies that possess numerous internal boundaries prone to microcracking during room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Introduce 0.5–1.0 wt% boron during alloy processing.
generation.conditions: Standard processing to achieve the eutectic dual-phase lamellar microstructure and subsequent room-temperature tensile deformation tests.
generation.structural_mediator: Boron segregation at the colony interfaces leading to either the formation of fine boride precipitates or an altered interfacial chemistry that reinforces the boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Boron atoms preferentially segregate to the colony (interphase) boundaries during processing, which enhances interfacial cohesion. This modification strengthens the barriers against dislocation motion (increasing strength) and mitigates early microcrack initiation (improving ductility) by preventing brittle interfacial failure, thus promoting effective load transfer and work hardening.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified baseline, the boron-added alloy is expected to exhibit a higher tensile strength and increased uniform elongation due to the enhanced interfacial strength and resistance to microcrack propagation.
generation.baseline: The unmodified eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibits limited ductility and premature microcrack initiation at the colony interfaces during room-temperature tensile testing.
generation.boundary: This beneficial effect is expected when the alloy maintains a fine, dual-phase lamellar structure; over-doping with boron or processing parameters that do not promote targeted boron segregation may lead to the formation of undesirable brittle intermetallic phases.
generation.uncertainty: The precise boron concentration window and the detailed nature of the interfacial phases (e.g., whether they form discrete borides or cause a general chemical strengthening) need further clarification. There is also some uncertainty regarding the balance between improved interface cohesion and any potential negative effects of excessive boron at the studied concentrations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of samples of the eutectic high-entropy alloy under identical processing conditions: one group with a 0.5–1.0 wt% boron addition and a control group without boron. Conduct microstructural characterizations (e.g., SEM, TEM, EBSD) to verify boron segregation at the colony interfaces. Then, perform standardized room-temperature tensile tests on both groups to compare overall strength, uniform elongation, and the onset of microcracking.
measurements: Microcrack density and initiation sites (via microscopy)
Distribution and chemistry of interfacial phases (via TEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-added samples do not show statistically significant improvements in both tensile strength and ductility compared to the control, or if microstructural analysis fails to demonstrate boron segregation at the interfaces, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractTo develop strong refractory high-entropy alloys for use at elevated temperatures as well as to overcome grain-boundary brittleness, an equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was prepared, and a minor amount of boron (0.1 at.%) was added into the alloy. The microstructures of the alloys were characterized, and their macro-to-microscale mechanical properties were measured. The microstructural observations indicated that the matrices of both the alloys were composed of a body-centered cubic solid-solution structure, and the added boron induced the precipitation of hexagonal close-packed borides (most likely the (Hf, Zr)B2) at the grain boundaries. The modulus and hardness of differently oriented grains were about equivalent, suggesting a diminished anisotropy, and many small slips occurred on multiple {110} planes. While the hardness of the matrix was not increased, the intergranular precipitation of the borides markedly raised the hardness of the grain boundaries. Owing to the enhanced grain boundary cohesion, the work hardenability and ductility were effectively improved with the addition of boron.Keywords: refractory alloy, high-entropy alloy, boride, grain boundary, mechanical prop

cited_evidence.text: From the small mixing enthalpies between each of the two elements given above and the great contribution of the high mixing entropy, the formation of a simple solid-solution structure without intermetallic compounds is expected, as also identified by the XRD and EBSD analyses in Figure 1. The XRD patterns in Figure 1a indicate the formation of a single-phase BCC structure in both the RHEA and RHEA-B samples. Owing to the higher cohesive energy of boron to the metallic elements than that of the metallic-to-metallic constituents [], a smaller lattice parameter was expected, and thus a slight shift of the diffraction peaks to a higher angle was observed upon the addition of boron. However, as more carefully characterized in the SEM image and EBSD phase map in Figure 1b,c, besides the major BCC phase composing the matrix of the RHEA-B sample, the minor addition of boron segregating at the grain boundaries was observed to induce the intergranular precipitation of the second phase (hexagonal close-packed, HCP) along the grain boundaries although the amount of the second phase was too small to be efficiently identified in the XRD analyses.

An equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr RHEA was developed in this study, and the addition of a minor amount of boron (0.1 at.%, RHEA-B) further overcame the grain-boundary brittleness. As indicated by the microstructural observations and chemical analyses, a simple BCC-phase, solid-solution structure was formed in the matrices of both the alloys. The addition of boron did not obviously increase the hardness of the matrix but induced the intergranular precipitation of the HCP-phase (Hf, Zr)B2 borides which markedly raised the hardness of the grain boundaries. Attributable to the lattice distortions caused by the random distribution of different constituent elements, a diminished anisotropy in the mechanical properties was noticed, and the deformation behavior was mediated by many small slips on multiple {110} planes. Owing to the enhanced grain boundary cohesion with the addition of boron and the intergranular precipitation of borides, the work hardenability and ductility of the alloy were effectively improved, and the failure mode obviously changed from a mainly intergranular facture to a major portion of the transgranular fracture.
